questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
questions.prompt: Only VMs in subnet Apps of VNet1 must reach a storage account's blob endpoint. What must you configure?
options: A virtual network rule for subnet Apps, with a Microsoft.Storage service endpoint enabled on that subnet
An IP network rule for the subnet's address range 10.1.1.0/24
A resource lock on the storage account
A stored access policy on the container
questions.explanation: Virtual network rules allow specific subnets. The subnet needs a Microsoft.Storage (or Microsoft.Storage.Global) service endpoint; the portal adds it for you when you add the rule.
why_not: IP rules accept only public IP addresses; private ranges are rejected.
Locks protect the resource from change; they don't filter network traffic.
A stored access policy constrains SAS tokens, not networks.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
questions.prompt: An IP network rule allows your company's public IP. A VM in the same Azure region as the storage account, with no service endpoint, isn't covered by any rule. Why can't you use an IP rule to control that VM's access?
options: IP rules only work with IPv6
The VM must use a SAS instead
IP network rules have no effect on requests from the same Azure region, which use private Azure addresses
IP rules apply only to SMB traffic
questions.explanation: Same-region requests use private addresses, so IP rules can't govern them. Use a virtual network rule for the VM's subnet.
why_not: Storage firewall IP rules support only IPv4.
SAS is authorization, not network filtering; it doesn't change which network rules apply.
Network rules apply to all protocols, REST and SMB.

questions.sub_skill: Configure Azure Storage firewalls and virtual networks
questions.prompt: After you set a storage account to allow only selected networks, you can still change its settings in the portal but can no longer list blobs in the portal's Containers view. Why?
options: You lost your Owner role when the firewall was enabled
The firewall blocks all portal traffic
Blob listing requires the account key to be regenerated
The firewall applies to data-plane operations; changing settings is control plane, but reading blobs in the portal is data plane
questions.explanation: Firewall rules restrict data-plane access only. Add your client IP to browse data from the portal.
why_not: Firewall rules don't change role assignments.
Management operations still work; only data access is filtered.
Key regeneration is unrelated to network rules.

questions.sub_skill: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
questions.prompt: An external partner needs read access to one blob for two days. You must not share account keys, and you want the most secure SAS type Microsoft recommends. What should you issue?
options: An account SAS
A user delegation SAS
The storage account connection string
An ad hoc service SAS valid for one year
questions.explanation: A user delegation SAS is signed with Microsoft Entra credentials rather than a key. Its maximum validity is 7 days, which covers two days.
why_not: An account SAS is signed with the account key; Microsoft recommends a user delegation SAS where possible.
That contains an account key and grants full access to all data.
It's key-signed and far longer than needed.

questions.sub_skill: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
questions.prompt: Which statement about a user delegation SAS is correct?
options: It can reference a stored access policy
It's signed with key2 by default
It works only for Blob Storage
It's valid for at most 7 days, and regenerating the account keys doesn't invalidate it
questions.explanation: A user delegation SAS lasts up to 7 days regardless of any SAS expiration policy. Key rotation doesn't affect it, because no account key signs it.
why_not: Stored access policies work only with a service SAS.
It's signed with a user delegation key obtained with Entra credentials, not an account key.
It's supported for Blob, Queue, Table and Azure Files.

questions.sub_skill: Create and use shared access signature (SAS) tokens
questions.prompt: You need a SAS that allows a tool to call Get Service Properties and to work across the Blob and Queue services. Which SAS type do you need?
options: An account SAS
A service SAS
A user delegation SAS
A service SAS with a stored access policy
questions.explanation: An account SAS can span one or more services and delegate service-level operations such as Get or Set Service Properties.
why_not: A service SAS covers one resource in one service and can't delegate service-level operations.
A user delegation SAS can't delegate the service-level operations an account SAS can.
It's still a service SAS: one service, no service-level operations.

questions.prompt: You've issued 40 service SAS tokens for container reports, all referencing stored access policy readers. One token has leaked. You must invalidate the tokens without disrupting anything else that uses the account keys. What should you do?
options: Regenerate key1 and key2
Delete the leaked SAS token from the storage account
Delete or rename the stored access policy (or set its expiry in the past), then issue new tokens under a new policy
Revoke the user delegation keys
questions.explanation: Changing or removing the stored access policy revokes every service SAS that references it, without touching the account keys.
why_not: That works, but it breaks every other application and SAS that uses the keys.
SAS tokens aren't stored or tracked; there's nothing to delete.
These are service SAS tokens signed with an account key; user delegation keys are unrelated.

questions.prompt: You deleted stored access policy readers to revoke some leaked tokens. A week later a colleague re-creates a policy named readers with a future expiry. What happens to the old tokens?
options: They stay revoked permanently
Tokens that referenced readers and haven't otherwise expired become valid again
They're converted to user delegation SAS tokens
They work only from the original client IP
questions.explanation: A SAS references the policy by name. Re-create a revoked policy under a new name.
why_not: Microsoft documents that re-creating a policy with the same name revives the associated tokens.
SAS types never convert.
Nothing about the policy re-creation adds an IP restriction.

questions.prompt: How many stored access policies can you define on a single blob container, and which SAS type can use them?
options: Up to five; only a service SAS
Unlimited; any SAS type
One; account SAS only
Five; user delegation SAS only
questions.explanation: A container supports up to five stored access policies, and only a service SAS can be associated with one.
why_not: There's a limit of five, and only a service SAS can reference one.
An account SAS must be ad hoc.
User delegation SAS tokens don't support stored access policies.

questions.prompt: An ad hoc account SAS signed with key1 has been posted publicly. It expires in three months. What is the only way to invalidate it immediately?
options: Delete the stored access policy
Revoke the user delegation keys
Set a SAS expiration policy on the account
Regenerate key1
questions.explanation: Regenerating the key that signed an ad hoc SAS is the only way to revoke it immediately.
why_not: An account SAS can't use a stored access policy.
This SAS was signed with key1, not a user delegation key.
An expiration policy warns about long validity at creation; it doesn't revoke existing tokens.

questions.prompt: You must rotate a storage account's keys without interrupting applications that use key1. What is the correct sequence?
options: Switch applications to key2, regenerate key1, switch applications back to key1, then regenerate key2
Regenerate both keys, then update the applications
Regenerate key1 while applications still use it
Disable Shared Key access, rotate, then enable it again
questions.explanation: Two keys exist so one is always valid: move clients to the other key, regenerate, and repeat.
why_not: Applications fail between the regeneration and the update.
The applications fail as soon as key1 changes.
That blocks all key-based access, so the applications fail too.

questions.prompt: Security requires that no one can access a storage account's data with account keys, including through SAS tokens signed with them, and that Conditional Access can protect it. What should you configure?
options: A key expiration policy of 1 day
A ReadOnly lock on the storage account
Disallow Shared Key authorization (AllowSharedKeyAccess = false)
Deny all networks in the firewall
questions.explanation: With Shared Key disallowed, requests authorized with an account key, including service and account SAS, fail with 403. Microsoft also requires it before Conditional Access can protect the account.
why_not: A key expiration policy is only a rotation reminder; keys keep working.
A ReadOnly lock blocks listing keys, but anyone who already has a key can still use it on the data plane.
That blocks every client, including Entra-authorized ones.

questions.sub_skill: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
questions.prompt: Users with Microsoft Entra-joined Windows devices and hybrid identities must access an Azure file share with their own credentials. The devices have no network line of sight to domain controllers. Which identity source should you enable?
options: On-premises AD DS
Microsoft Entra Kerberos
Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Storage account key
questions.explanation: Microsoft Entra Kerberos issues the Kerberos tickets itself, so clients don't need domain controller line of sight. Hybrid identities still need an AD DS synced to Microsoft Entra ID.
why_not: AD DS authentication requires clients to reach the domain controllers.
Clients must be joined to the managed domain and reach its domain controllers.
A key isn't an identity source and gives every user full access.

questions.sub_skill: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
questions.prompt: AD DS authentication is enabled for a storage account, but the on-premises identities are NOT synced to Microsoft Entra ID. All authenticated users must get read access to every share, with Windows ACLs providing finer control. What should you configure?
options: Assign Storage File Data SMB Share Reader to each user in Azure RBAC
A stored access policy on each share
Nothing: the default share-level permission already grants read
The default share-level permission, set to Storage File Data SMB Share Reader
questions.explanation: The default share-level permission applies to all authenticated identities, needs no sync, and covers every share in the account. Windows ACLs then enforce file and directory permissions.
why_not: RBAC share-level assignments need identities that exist in Microsoft Entra ID.
That's for SAS tokens, not SMB identity access.
The default share-level permission is None until you set it.

questions.sub_skill: Configure identity-based access for Azure Files
questions.prompt: A user holds Storage File Data SMB Share Contributor on a share but gets access denied when opening the share's root folder. What is the most likely cause?
options: The role must be Storage Blob Data Contributor
Identity-based access supports only NFS shares
Windows ACLs on the root directory don't grant the user access; the share-level role only admits them to the share
The share needs a second identity source
questions.explanation: Access needs both a share-level permission and file or directory permissions. Azure Files enforces Windows ACLs, including on the root directory.
why_not: Blob roles don't apply to Azure Files SMB access.
It supports SMB shares; NFS isn't supported.
A storage account can use only one identity source.
